forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.83 represents a 2.2% premium to Street consensus of $1.79, a slight reduction from my prior $1.84 estimate reflecting more conservative SG&A normalization assumptions. The Street has correctly identified tax rate normalization as the primary mechanical headwind - Q4's 10.3% effective rate was anomalously low and should normalize to ~22% - but I believe consensus is still too bearish on three key factors: (1) SG&A should normalize from Q4's elevated $955M to ~$880M as one-time transformation costs roll off, providing ~$0.05 tailwind; (2) cold/flu seasonal strength is tracking above normal per CDC data, supporting ~$140M sequential tissue revenue uplift; (3) discontinued operations from Brazil should contribute ~$115M, slightly moderating the tax normalization impact.

The institutional flow data validates this above-consensus view. Jain Global's new $12M stake and BMO's 17.8% position increase suggest sophisticated investors see value the Street is missing. While CalPERS' partial exit (17.6% reduction) introduces a counterpoint, pension funds often rebalance for non-fundamental reasons. The Powering Care transformation continues delivering with management confirming an 8th consecutive quarter of positive volume+mix in Q4 - I expect this extends to a 9th quarter in Q1 2026. The ethics recognition (World's Most Ethical Companies for 8th consecutive year) is neutral to earnings but reinforces brand equity in an ESG-conscious environment.

My conviction is medium rather than high because the tax rate normalization creates meaningful uncertainty. If the effective rate exceeds 22.5% or discontinued operations contribution moderates faster than expected, my estimate could be too aggressive. Conversely, if SG&A normalization is more pronounced than modeled (~$860M vs my $880M), EPS could exceed $1.85. The key swing factor remains the magnitude of tax normalization versus operational improvement - I believe the Street is overweighting the former and underweighting the latter.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 FY2026 forecast of -$0.02 EPS on $76.5M revenue maintains a DIFFERENTIATED VIEW from the historical 4-quarter average consensus of -$0.04 EPS. The Street appears to be over-weighting Q1's disastrous -$0.25 EPS result without recognizing that this was a one-time shock from California's $4/hour minimum wage increase hitting simultaneously across all California locations on January 1. By Q2, management has had a full quarter to adjust pricing, optimize labor scheduling, and absorb the wage step-up into normalized operations. The February news that traffic actually IMPROVED despite a 3.5% price hike provides critical evidence that Kura's value proposition and 52% loyalty penetration gives them pricing power other casual dining chains lack.

The key data points supporting my variant view: (1) Q4 2025 achieved 13.7% gross margin and +$0.19 EPS, proving the operating model works when labor costs are stable; (2) Management's track record shows Q1 misses are often timing-driven rather than structural - Q2 2025 also had a -$0.31 EPS followed by Q3's +$0.05 recovery; (3) New unit contribution of 4 stores opened in Q1 will add $5-6M of incremental revenue in Q2, supporting topline growth to $76.5M from Q1's $73.5M. My Q1 2026 forecast maintains the -$0.15 EPS estimate (approximately KRW -168B net loss), materially divergent from the implied Street consensus of +$0.18 EPS. The fundamental disconnect is that Wall Street appears to be modeling off operating income improvements without properly accounting for the substantial non-operating cost structure. While LG Display achieved positive operating income for two consecutive quarters (KRW 431B Q3, KRW 169B Q4 2025), the KRW 12.7T debt burden generates approximately KRW 155B quarterly in interest expense that structurally prevents positive EPS. Q1 faces the additional headwind of typical 11% seasonal revenue decline, which drives operating deleverage and compresses operating income back toward breakeven.

The UDC partnership renewal is strategically positive but provides no incremental financial benefit to Q1. Photronics results confirm stable but not accelerating display demand.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of significant interest expense reduction through refinancing at materially lower rates; (2) Better-than-expected panel pricing recovery evidenced by industry data; (3) Material shift in OLED product mix toward higher-margin IT/automotive panels. Until I see structural improvement in the non-operating cost structure, positive EPS remains mathematically unlikely despite operational progress.

Institutional flows remain supportive with Gotham Asset Management increasing stakes 55.3% and Alliancebernstein adding 6.8%.

The Street appears to be modeling a more conservative tax rate assumption or not fully crediting the volume stabilization trend. My confidence is medium given the tax rate is the swing factor and there is inherent uncertainty around regulatory timing.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.55 is modestly above the Street consensus of $1.53 (+1.3%), reflecting a balanced view that incorporates both supportive crack spread fundamentals and concerning institutional/insider selling patterns. The key bullish factor is Gulf Coast 3:2:1 crack spreads holding at $15-16/bbl versus $10-12/bbl in Q1 2025, which should translate to materially better realized margins year-over-year. Management's Q4 2025 earnings call highlighted 105% margin capture and strong operational execution, suggesting the team can extract value even in challenging seasonal periods.

However, I've reduced my estimate from $1.58 to $1.55 due to accumulating bearish signals that warrant attention. The CCO's insider sale of 1,626 shares (17.77% of holdings) follows the pattern of institutional selling (L2 Asset Management down 46.9%, Ameriprise down 19.3%). While some institutions are adding (Aquatic +618%, KKM +27.6%), the net sentiment has shifted more cautious. Additionally, the consensus estimate dropped sharply from $1.74 to $1.53 over four days, suggesting Street analysts may have insight into deteriorating near-term fundamentals I haven't fully captured. Q1 seasonal dynamics remain the primary headwind - turnaround activity compresses utilization to 90-91% from Q4's 94%, and working capital typically consumes cash in Q1.

I would revise my estimate lower if: (1) we see evidence of crack spread compression below $14/bbl, (2) turnaround complications are reported extending planned downtime, or (3) additional large institutional sells are filed. Conversely, I'd move higher if crack spreads strengthen toward $18/bbl or turnaround execution proves better than guided. My conviction is medium given the conflicting signals between supportive commodity fundamentals and cautionary institutional behavior.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 FY26 estimate of $4.38 EPS on $88.2B revenue represents a 8.1% premium to Street consensus EPS of $4.05, reflecting continued conviction that Wall Street systematically underestimates Microsoft's AI monetization trajectory and operating leverage. The Q2 FY26 EPS surprise of +32% demonstrated that the AI thesis is not merely theoretical but is now showing up in actual financial results through both Azure consumption acceleration and Copilot enterprise adoption. Oracle's Q3 2026 RPO surge to $553B provides critical independent validation that hyperscale cloud demand remains robust, directly benefiting Azure's infrastructure business. The institutional activity in today's news - minor position trims by GM Advisory Group (-1.9%) and Kozak & Associates (-5.5%) alongside increases by Silvant Capital (+3.9%) - represents normal portfolio rebalancing rather than any shift in fundamental view, as MSFT remains a top holding across these funds.

The key variant perception driving my above-consensus view centers on three pillars: (1) Azure AI contribution is now 15+ percentage points of Azure's 29-31% growth, with enterprise customers locked into consumption-based agreements that create durable revenue streams; (2) Copilot is reaching inflection with an estimated 12-15M seats generating $1.3-1.5B quarterly run-rate, and the Street is modeling closer to $900M-1.1B; (3) Operating leverage from the high-margin AI software mix is expanding operating margins toward 49.5%, up from the Street's expectation of ~48%. Microsoft's gross margins should expand to 68.5% as software/services outpace lower-margin hardware, while D&A pressure is moderating as infrastructure buildout growth rate stabilizes. The risk to my thesis would be clear evidence of Azure consumption deceleration below 28% or enterprise Copilot churn - neither of which appears in current channel data. I would reduce my estimate if Q3 guidance suggests any moderation in AI-driven growth or if CapEx intensity remains at Q2's elevated $30B+ level without corresponding revenue uplift.

Conversely, if D&A comes in below $13B due to different capex timing, our EPS estimate would be too conservative. We monitor competitive cloud pricing and AI workload adoption as key swing factors.

My FCF estimate of $65M reflects significant working capital normalization as receivables and inventory decline with lower sequential revenue.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of customer destocking or order delays beyond normal seasonality, (2) gross margin deterioration below 40% suggesting pricing pressure, or (3) PMI data collapsing below 46 indicating manufacturing recession. The Street's $0.84 consensus appears to adequately reflect macro headwinds but may slightly underestimate MSC's operational leverage. My modest above-consensus call reflects continued confidence in execution rather than any expectation of demand recovery.

My conviction remains medium rather than high because Q4 2025 results are now overdue (we're in mid-March 2026), and any deviation in actual OpEx from my normalization thesis would meaningfully impact EPS given the tight margins. If R&D spending was elevated in Q4 for early Phase 3 preparation, my estimate could prove too optimistic.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.95 represents a 2.2% premium to Street consensus of $0.93, driven by Nasdaq's persistent pattern of conservative guidance and systematic analyst underestimation. The company has delivered positive EPS surprises in 5 consecutive quarters with an average beat of 4.3%, yet analysts continue to anchor conservatively. Key to my above-consensus view is the strength in Index Solutions, evidenced by continued Citigroup and JPMorgan 424B2 filings through mid-March for Nasdaq-100 linked structured products, which I estimate contributes ~$180M to Q1 revenue. The March 1 Investor Day reinforced management confidence with new growth targets, $3B buyback authorization, and expanded strategic initiatives in AI, cloud, and blockchain.

The primary headwind for Q1 is the normalization of the effective tax rate from Q4's anomalous 10.5% to approximately 19%, which will drive ~$40M higher tax expense sequentially. However, this is well-understood by the Street and fully embedded in consensus. My revenue estimate of $2.11B reflects modest sequential decline from Q4's $2.08B (seasonal Q1 softness in trading) but solid year-over-year growth of approximately 1% driven by Solutions businesses. Operating margins should remain stable around 27.5% as the business continues its mix shift toward higher-margin recurring revenue streams.

What would make me change my view: (1) Evidence of material trading volume weakness beyond normal Q1 seasonality, (2) Index AUM outflows reversing the structured product demand trend, or (3) Management commentary suggesting higher-than-expected investment spending. I maintain medium-high conviction given the predictable nature of Nasdaq's recurring revenue streams and management's consistent track record of conservative guidance. The February volumes report showed no material deviation from expectations, and no negative fundamental news has emerged since my prior analysis.

My forecast of $0.97 EPS (vs consensus $0.93) is predicated on the market under-modeling the durability of Nasdaq's margin transformation. The Q4 drop in Cost of Revenue (from ~$1.1B to $688M) was not a fluke but a structural shift to 'Net Reporting' that permanently elevates gross margins to ~67%. While Wall Street is distracted by Q4's noisy OpEx ($917M 'Other Expenses'), Q1 will reveal the clean earnings power: moderate revenue growth (~5% YoY) flowing through this new, more efficient margin structure.

However, I have tempered my previous $1.02 bullish call. The mathematical reality is that Q4's 10.5% effective tax rate was a significant tailwind that will reverse in Q1 (modeling 19%). Additionally, the soft transaction volume signals from February introduce a revenue risk factor that wasn't present in prior assumptions. The convergence of a structural margin breakout with a tax/volume seasonal headwind lands us at a conviction beat of $0.04, rather than a blowout.

Key variation from consensus lies in the Operating Margin. I expect normalized Operating Margins to expand toward 35% (up from historical low-30s) as the Cost of Revenue accounting change sticks. If Q1 Cost of Revenue reverts to >$1B, my thesis is broken, but Q4 evidence suggests this is the new standard.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.44 remains 52.2% BELOW Wall Street consensus of $0.92, reflecting what I believe is a critical analytical failure by the Street to properly model NextEra's pronounced quarterly seasonality. The evidence is overwhelming and unchanged: Q1 2025 delivered diluted EPS of just $0.40 despite full-year 2025 EPS of approximately $3.55 - meaning Q1 represented only ~11% of annual earnings. This pattern is structural and recurring due to two factors: (1) FPL experiences its lowest electricity demand in Q1 as Florida's mild winter reduces both heating and cooling needs, and (2) NEER's wind portfolio operates at seasonal trough capacity factors of 28-30% versus 35-40% in peak quarters.

The March 2026 news flow shows continued institutional position rebalancing (Faithward Advisors selling 70.1% of position, Danske Bank acquiring 1.17M shares, CIBC increasing stake 1.9%), but this backward-looking Q3 2025 data is noise for Q1 earnings purposes. The key earnings call insights remain unchanged: management confirmed 8% long-term growth guidance, 30GW data center target by 2035, and FPL rate base growth on track. However, none of these long-term positives change the fundamental Q1 seasonality. Interest expense normalization from Q1 2025's anomalous $1.77B to projected $620M provides meaningful tailwind, but cannot overcome the 35-40% revenue and earnings compression inherent in Q1.

I would change my view if: (1) management provided explicit Q1 guidance materially different from historical patterns, (2) there was evidence of major one-time gains from asset sales or tax items, or (3) weather data showed unusual Q1 demand patterns in Florida. None of these conditions exist. The Street appears to be applying annual earnings run-rates without proper quarterly adjustment, a systematic error that creates alpha opportunity for those who model granularly.

The $148M in proceeds used for debt paydown reduces interest expense by ~$3M quarterly going forward.

The transformation thesis remains intact with no new material information since my March 17 analysis. Institutional accumulation continues with ArrowMark increasing holdings 28.5% and Teton Advisors initiating a new position, offsetting Clarkston's 16.5% reduction. The stock's volatility (hitting $9.63 intraday low) reflects market uncertainty about the transformation, but no fundamental issues have emerged. Food Safety regulatory headwinds mentioned in news appear to be sector-wide and not Neogen-specific, with no near-term earnings impact evident.

My conviction remains medium due to binary transaction timing risk - if the Zoetis deal slips to Q4, my thesis is completely wrong and EPS would be around -$0.07. However, no delays have been announced through March 17, regulatory approvals appear on track, and management has maintained mid-Q3 close guidance. The Street's persistent $0.02 consensus suggests they may be sandbagging the gain or not modeling it at all, creating significant upside if the transaction closes as expected.

forecasts.thesis:
I maintain a contrarian Buy rating/Forecast on NEOG for Q3 2026, driven primarily by a revenue recognition arbitrage opportunity that the Street is currently mispricing. The Consensus estimate of $210M implies that the Genomics divestiture (signed March 2, 2026) has already been removed from Top Line results for Q3 (ended Feb 28). However, US GAAP (ASC 205-20) dictates that because the Definitive Agreement was signed *after* the quarter close, the revenue (~$15M impact) should remain in Continuing Operations for this reporting period. This creates a structural 'technical beat' setup where reported revenue hits ~$219M vs $210M expectations.

However, I have tempered my previous bullishness on the EPS line compared to yesterday's forecast. New analysis of news from March 16 confirming 'regulatory headwinds' and 'price pressure' in the core Food Safety business suggests that the organic lift will be muted. While the accounting technicality secures the revenue beat, operational friction and one-time transaction costs (legal/advisory) buried in SG&A will dampen the EPS flow-through. I forecast Adjusted EPS of $0.04, beating consensus ($0.02) largely on volume leverage from the 'extra' revenue line, but remaining conservative on margins.

My thesis would be invalidated if Neogen management classifies the Genomics business as 'Held for Sale' retroactively based on intent prior to Feb 28, moving revenue to Discontinued Operations. This would align reported revenue with consensus ($210M), removing the catalyst.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.62 remains 43% below the Wall Street consensus of $2.84, a significant divergence that reflects my conviction that the Street is systematically mispricing Nucor's structural margin compression. The critical evidence supporting my variant view: (1) Cost of revenue has been stuck at 88-89% for four consecutive quarters, with no improvement despite stable steel pricing; (2) Q4 2025's -23.4% earnings miss ($1.64 vs $2.14 expected) was dismissed by the market as an anomaly when it was actually confirmation of this cost structure problem; (3) Cleveland-Cliffs' emergency plant idlings and Ternium's headwinds confirm broader steel sector demand weakness that Nucor cannot fully escape.

The Steel Dynamics Q1 guidance does provide some positive signal - their $2.73-2.77 EPS range (though 15% below Street at $3.24) represents near-doubling YoY and suggests infrastructure/data center spending is providing sector support. This gives me slightly more confidence to raise my estimate from $1.58 to $1.62. However, STLD also missed consensus by 15%, reinforcing that Wall Street is systematically too optimistic on steel margins. The Street appears anchored on Nucor's historical 83-85% CoR levels that no longer apply in the current cost environment.

What would make me change my mind: (1) If Nucor reports CoR below 87%, I would significantly revise upward as this would indicate the structural cost issues are resolving; (2) If shipment volumes surprise materially above seasonal norms (suggesting demand is stronger than Cleveland-Cliffs' actions imply); (3) If management provides guidance suggesting margin recovery in H2 2026. Until I see concrete evidence of cost structure improvement, I maintain my substantially below-consensus view with medium conviction.

My variant view is that Q2 FY2026 is still primarily a timing/acceptance quarter: revenue can land modestly above the $0.35B consensus without implying a durable demand inflection. The recent OriginAI/MemoryAI announcements and the Dell/Deepgram collaboration are strategically positive, but they are not sufficiently quantified to assume a material near-quarter conversion; I treat them as pipeline/relevance builders rather than immediate revenue accelerants.

Where I differ most from the Street is on earnings quality: with operating income relatively stable, quarterly EPS is unusually sensitive to non-operating swings (as seen in recent quarters). forecasts.thesis:
I am raising my Q1 2026 EPS estimate from $0.58 to $0.63, though this remains 18% below Wall Street consensus of $0.77. My key differentiated view: I believe the Street is over-extrapolating Pfizer's exceptional beat streak (five consecutive quarters of 15-41% beats) into Q1, which is structurally the company's weakest seasonal quarter. COVID products - including Comirnaty vaccines and Paxlovid treatments - see their lowest demand in Q1 as flu/respiratory season winds down. Q4 2025's $17.56B revenue was boosted by peak vaccination season; Q1 should normalize closer to Q1 2025's $13.71B, though I'm modeling modest growth to $14.25B reflecting oncology strength.

The persistent beat pattern is the key analytical puzzle. Pfizer has beaten consensus by 15%+ for five straight quarters, suggesting either: (1) analysts are systematically conservative, (2) there are operational efficiencies not captured in models, or (3) one-time benefits are inflating reported EPS. I've increased my estimate to account for this pattern, but I refuse to simply assume a 30%+ beat will recur. The Q4 2025 loss of $0.29 EPS was driven by non-operating charges ($5.33B in other expenses, likely impairments), making that quarter anomalous. Q1 should return to normalized profitability, but at a lower level than the Street expects given seasonal revenue headwinds.

My conviction is medium-high. The Phase 2 atirmociclib success for breast cancer and tilrekimig for atopic dermatitis strengthen the long-term pipeline narrative but contribute zero to Q1 2026 revenue. What would change my view: evidence that Paxlovid demand is holding up better than seasonal patterns suggest (potentially from ongoing COVID waves), or if gross margins prove more resilient than the 68% I'm modeling. The 28-analyst consensus at $0.77 implies the Street believes the beat streak continues - I think they're underweighting Q1's structural challenges.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $0.03 remains 40% below the Wall Street consensus of $0.05, reflecting Richardson Electronics' fundamental structural constraint: the company cannot generate meaningful operating leverage on its fixed SG&A base of approximately $15.7M per quarter. This pattern has been remarkably consistent—Q2 2026 posted a net loss on $52.3M revenue with $15.9M SG&A, while Q1 2026 achieved only $0.13 EPS on stronger $54.6M revenue. The Street appears to be extrapolating from Q1's strength without recognizing that quarter benefited from timing-related revenue pull-forward that reversed in Q2. My $53M revenue forecast represents modest sequential improvement as PMT semiconductor/RF destocking pressure stabilizes, but remains insufficient to overcome the SG&A cost structure that requires approximately $55M+ revenue to generate meaningful earnings.

The key differentiated insight is that Richardson's cost structure is essentially immutable—SG&A has remained in the $15.5-16.0M range for eight consecutive quarters regardless of revenue levels. Management has shown no willingness or ability to rationalize this expense base, meaning profitability is entirely dependent on revenue exceeding the ~$54-55M threshold where gross profit covers fixed costs with margin to spare. At $53M revenue with 31% gross margin, gross profit of ~$16.4M barely exceeds SG&A of ~$15.7M, leaving minimal operating income before other items. The LaserSlat SAVER product launch on March 10 is incrementally positive but represents a distribution agreement for a consumable product—the ramp to meaningful revenue contribution is measured in quarters, not weeks, making Q3 impact negligible.

I would revise my estimate upward if: (1) revenue surprises above $55M indicating PMT recovery is stronger than expected, (2) SG&A comes in below $15.5M suggesting cost discipline, or (3) LaserSlat SAVER adoption proves faster than anticipated. However, none of these scenarios is supported by current evidence. The consensus at $0.05 requires ~$55M+ revenue or margin improvement that historical patterns simply do not support.

SG&A could exceed $16M if Q4 merit increases are front-loaded

My Q3 2026 forecast of $0.02 EPS on $106M revenue represents a critical inflection point where RGP transitions from deep losses to near-breakeven through aggressive cost restructuring rather than top-line recovery. The Street consensus of $0.04 EPS appears achievable but may be slightly optimistic given the execution risk on SG&A realization. My differentiated view centers on the mechanics of the January 2026 workforce reduction: I project ~$14M in Q3 SG&A savings (from $54.4M in Q2 to $40M), consisting of approximately $8M in actual run-rate headcount savings and $6M in one-time severance accrual reversal. This cost action should offset the gross profit decline from revenue falling to $106M.

The key data points driving my thesis are: (1) Q2 2026 SG&A spiked to $54.4M from $47.9M in Q1, suggesting restructuring-related charges that should reverse in Q3; (2) Revenue trajectory shows -2% QoQ in Q1 but acceleration to -10% in Q2 as macro headwinds intensified; (3) Working capital continues releasing cash as receivables decline proportionally with revenue, supporting liquidity despite losses; (4) Strategic hires (Boyer for M&A, Garcia for Finance Transformation, Friedman for Tax/Treasury) signal management's pivot to higher-margin consulting but these won't contribute meaningfully until late FY2026 or FY2027.

I would change my view if: (1) Q3 revenue comes in below $100M, indicating demand deterioration worse than projected; (2) SG&A remains elevated above $45M, suggesting restructuring savings are delayed; or (3) The company announces additional goodwill impairment, which would indicate management's view of the business has deteriorated further. My medium confidence reflects the binary nature of the restructuring payoff - either the cost cuts flow through as modeled, producing near-breakeven, or execution delays result in another loss quarter around -$0.10 EPS.

I am forecasting Q1 2026 Adjusted EPS of $1.57, beating the consensus of $1.51, and Revenue of $22.88B. My variant view is anchored in two specific areas where the 'weak Q1 seasonality' narrative is overshadowing structural tailwinds. First, the Commercial Aftermarket segment (Collins/Pratt) is seeing pricing realization catch up to inflation faster than Wall Street models, which will drive margin expansion even on seasonally lower volumes. Second, while the specific Alabama missile facility only came online March 13 (limiting its Q1 revenue contribution), the *inventory build* preceding this (as seen in Q4 working capital data) suggests Raytheon has been prepping for a delivery surge that will be recognized earlier in the cycle than typical percentage-of-completion models suggest.

My revenue forecast of $22.88B represents stable sequential performance relative to historical Q4->Q1 drops, acknowledging the Alabama timing but crediting the robust aftermarket demand. The consensus seems to be over-penalizing for the seasonality without giving enough credit to the 'Golden Dome' expenditure ramp and the $4.7B Egypt deal which provide concrete backlog support. The recent 20% stake increase by Mackenzie Financial and 50% by BMO supports the institutional accumulation view that I share.

I would revisit this thesis if we see signs of GTF engine groundings increasing beyond current projections (350 aircraft), as this would shift the mix from high-margin aftermarket spares to lower-margin warranty/support work. Additionally, any new supply chain bottlenecks in titanium could stall the delivery of high-ticket OE units, although this is more of a risk to revenue than earnings due to the lower margins on OE.

The payout ratio exceeds 130%, meaning Saratoga is paying dividends from capital rather than earnings. The ATM program (issuing ~2% more shares per quarter) is a temporary band-aid that dilutes existing shareholders. I believe the Street is underweighting this structural cash flow problem while overweighting recent operating expense normalization.

My estimate could prove too conservative if: (1) realized gains from portfolio exits materialize this quarter, (2) fee income surprises positively from deal restructurings, or (3) credit quality remains pristine despite macro headwinds. Conversely, I would revise lower if cash burn accelerates further or if management signals dividend stress. The 8-K filings suggest routine business activity, but I'm watching closely for any signals of portfolio stress or strategic shifts in capital allocation.

My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.38 remains 5.6% above Street consensus of $0.36, maintained from my previous forecast as no material new data has emerged to alter my core thesis. The primary source of alpha in this call is the mechanical EPS accretion from aggressive share buybacks - Q1 saw $99.6M in repurchases that increased treasury stock from $129.3M to $230M, implying approximately 6.3 million shares retired at an average price around $16. This brings my diluted share count estimate to approximately 78.2M for Q2, which is materially below where I believe the Street is modeling (likely still using 90-95M based on stale data). At $29.7M net income on 78.2M shares, that yields $0.38 EPS vs consensus $0.36.

The operational thesis is supported by recent sector data points. Smucker's Q3 2026 results showed 7% sales growth with pricing gains offsetting volume pressures, and Campbell's Q2 results demonstrated resilience in snacking categories. While SMPL operates in a more challenged weight management niche, the Jefferies upgrade to Buy with a $22 price target specifically validates the Quest brand strength thesis - they cite Quest driving 10% revenue growth over four years. I model Quest at +8% YoY and Atkins at -2% YoY (stabilizing from prior -5% trends), yielding total revenue of $345M vs consensus $340M. Gross margin recovery to 33.5% from Q1's depressed 32.3% reflects input cost normalization.

I have medium conviction given the mechanical nature of the buyback math, but acknowledge significant uncertainty around exact share count timing and treatment.

My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $8.15 represents a 58% sequential increase from Q2's $5.15, driven by SanDisk's continued transformation into an enterprise AI memory leader with exceptional operating leverage. The critical differentiated insight versus Wall Street is that the consensus $13.93 EPS figure appears to be either annualized, erroneous, or reflecting a different fiscal period - given the company's quarterly run-rate progression (Q4 2025: -$0.16, Q1 2026: $0.75, Q2 2026: $5.15), a jump to $13.93 in Q3 would require nearly 170% sequential growth which is unrealistic even with strong fundamentals. The key catalyst since my previous forecast is the confirmation of multi-year LTA (Long-Term Agreement) deals with hyperscalers, which provides both volume visibility and pricing power unprecedented in the commodity NAND industry. This news supports a modest upward revision from $7.92 to $8.15, as the LTA structure enables better enterprise ASP realization (+4% sequential vs. my prior +2% assumption) while securing volume commitments. The data center segment is now confirmed as SanDisk's largest end market, validating the structural shift thesis. Gross margins should expand to 53.5% driven by enterprise mix shift (now 45% of revenue) and LTA pricing benefits.

The primary risk to my thesis remains share dilution from stock-based compensation - I'm projecting diluted shares of ~136M for Q3, a 3.2% sequential increase that continues to erode per-share metrics despite strong operating performance. If the company accelerates SBC grants or the stock price appreciation creates larger equity dilution, EPS could come in 3-5% below my estimate. forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 FY2026 forecast of $2.85 non-GAAP diluted EPS on $15.42B revenue maintains a 5.6% discount to Wall Street consensus of $3.02 EPS and 9.0% below consensus revenue of $16.95B. The core differentiation remains my conviction that Street estimates fail to adequately price in the historical Q4-to-Q1 seasonal normalization pattern. TD SYNNEX consistently shows 10-15% sequential revenue declines from Q4 to Q1 as holiday-driven PC and endpoint demand normalizes, and Q4 FY2025's exceptional $17.38B revenue creates a particularly challenging comp. The stale consensus—unchanged at $3.02/$16.95B for over two weeks despite approaching earnings—suggests analysts have not fully modeled the seasonal dynamics.

I've raised my forecast modestly from $2.82/$15.35B based on two developments: (1) the SCAILIUM AI Infrastructure partnership announced February 24th signals healthy momentum in the advanced solutions channel, and (2) the March 3rd announcement of updated reportable segments—separating Hyve into its own disclosure—reduces uncertainty around AI infrastructure contribution and suggests management is confident enough in this segment to provide transparency. However, given the seasonal cash burn dynamics ($2B+ expected outflow) driving interest expenses up, the 'beat on revenue, miss on earnings' setup is high conviction.

More importantly, Dupixent's triple indication expansion (AFRS, COPD, CSU) is tracking ahead of Street models based on physician adoption data and competitor commentary on market share dynamics. The Q4 2025 earnings call highlighted €5.7B in new launch revenue and 9.9% sales growth, demonstrating execution that should carry into Q1 2026.

The Street appears to be extrapolating concerns from the 25% share price decline over the past year into earnings estimates, but I see this as sentiment-driven rather than fundamentally justified. CEO transition costs are deferred to Q2 per prior analysis, providing margin support this quarter. ALTUVIIIO's blockbuster achievement in 2025 validates the specialty care pivot strategy, and the in vivo mRNA CAR-T platform news (March 17) adds longer-term optionality that isn't priced in. My €11.15B revenue estimate reflects 5% YoY growth vs. Q1 2025's €10.61B, with specialty care strength offsetting vaccine seasonality.

Key risks to my thesis include: (1) FX headwinds exceeding my 2% assumption if EUR/USD moves adversely, (2) JAK inhibitor competitive pressure materializing faster than expected, and (3) any surprise R&D charges not telegraphed by management. I would lower my estimate if Dupixent channel checks showed inventory destocking or if competitor approvals accelerated in key indications. However, with 10 analysts maintaining Buy ratings and average target of $57.68 (~40% upside), institutional support remains intact despite sentiment weakness.

My forecast of $1.21 (Business EPS) materially exceeds the Street's $1.08. This divergence is driven by the structural pivot to 'Pure Play' biopharma, which the consensus model under-appreciates. Q1 2026 represents a 'Clean Quarter' where the resolution of the Amgen litigation (March 12) and the Medley divestiture (March 10) remove key overhangs. While the GAAP numbers will be noisy with divestiture gains and R&D upfronts (Sino Biopharm), the core underlying profitability is accelerating faster than modeled, led by Dupixent's continued 20%+ compounding and optimized OpEx.

The Street is likely over-penalizing for the Q1 seasonal step-down and potentially mis-modeling the net impact of the divestitures, seeing lost revenue without fully crediting the efficiency gains. My data suggests Dupixent's new indications are ramping faster than the conservative linear extrapolation seen in consensus. The $500M+ cash infusion from Medley further de-risks the balance sheet, allowing for sustained R&D investment without pressuring margins.

I would revisit this thesis if Dupixent prescription trends (IQVIA data) show an unexpected plateau or if the Sino Biopharm deal structure requires a larger-than-expected expense recognition in Business EPS (rather than just GAAP). However, with the Venglustat Breakthrough Therapy designation adding to the mid-to-long term valuation floor, the risk/reward for Q1 earnings is skewed to the upside.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 forecast of $2.75 EPS on $4.68B revenue aligns with the midpoint of Steel Dynamics' explicit guidance range of $2.73-$2.77 EPS issued on March 17, 2026. This represents a significant 13% miss versus the prior Wall Street consensus of $3.18, which I believe was materially too high. The Street's tariff-driven optimism failed to account for the timing lag between tariff implementation and actual margin realization. Today's news from multiple sources confirms the company is executing well on shipments and operational efficiency, but the full benefit of trade policy tailwinds has not yet materialized.

The key variance from consensus stems from gross margin assumptions. While the Street appeared to model 13%+ gross margins on tariff optimism, actual Q1 margins are running closer to 11.8% based on management's guidance range. Steel pricing has stabilized at $775-780/ton but hasn't seen the spike some analysts anticipated. The metals recycling and fabrication segments are contributing positively, but not enough to offset the core steel margin miss. Cleveland Cliffs' operational challenges (fraud investigation, six plants idled) represent a medium-term supply tailwind, but this benefit is more likely to manifest in Q2-Q3 rather than Q1.

My conviction is high given management's explicit guidance anchors the estimate within a narrow range. The primary upside scenario would be if margins came in at the high end of guidance ($2.77), while downside risk exists if working capital or tax timing creates drag. I would reassess if steel pricing shows meaningful movement above $800/ton or if management revises guidance prior to earnings. The 6% dividend increase announced in late February signals management confidence in cash generation, which supports the fundamental thesis.

Operational income is actually ramping sequentially.

I differ from the implied bearishness of the guidance by modeling slightly better metal spread capture. Steel Dynamics often guides using spot pricing that ignores intra-quarter improvements, and recent checks suggest HRC pricing stabilized faster in March than anticipated. Additionally, the 'Volume Super-Cycle' thesis isn't dead; it's just paused for capital reallocation. The inventory build I'm projecting ($3.85B) suggests management is preparing for a heavy shipment Q2 adjacent to tariff implementations.

Risks to my thesis include the acquisition falling through, which would leave the cash pile idle without the offsetting buyback benefit, or a faster-than-expected deterioration in fabrication margins. However, with Cleveland Cliffs idling plants, the supply side constraints provide a floor for STLD's pricing power that isn't fully reflected in the cautious $2.73 low-end guide.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 FY2026 EPS estimate of $2.01 remains 17% above Street consensus of $1.72, driven by systematic underestimation of mechanical EPS drivers that operate largely independent of top-line volatility. The consensus appears anchored on depressed sentiment following the Wine & Spirits divestiture and CEO transition (Nicholas Fink named March 8), creating a valuation discount driven by narrative rather than fundamentals. Three quantifiable factors support my above-consensus view: (1) accelerated share buybacks at depressed prices reducing diluted share count to ~170.8M from 174.6M in Q3, (2) declining interest expense to ~$82M from $86.6M in Q3 as debt paydown continues, and (3) SG&A normalization to ~$355M after Q3's $491M included one-time charges.

The Street appears to be extrapolating Q3's elevated SG&A as a new run-rate and failing to fully credit the mechanical EPS accretion from capital allocation discipline. Q3's reported EPS of $3.06 beat consensus by 10.1% primarily on these same factors. The beer segment remains resilient with Pacifico and Victoria continuing momentum despite flat to slightly negative volume trends, as price/mix offsets volume pressure. Revenue is capped at ~$2.17B by seasonal Q4 patterns (consistent with Q4 FY2025's $2.16B).

What would change my view: If SG&A remains elevated above $400M (indicating CEO transition costs are larger than assumed) or if share count reduction slows materially (suggesting buyback pace has decelerated). The Diageo short interest increase (+32.9%) and Brown-Forman underperformance validate STZ's strategic exit from spirits, but I remain alert to any tariff-related headline risk on Mexican imports that could pressure sentiment even if actual earnings impact is minimal.

While Wall Street consensus ($1.72) appears to be capitulating to the Spirits weakness narrative, it fundamentally ignores the arithmetic necessity of the tax rate arbitrage for FY26. Management's guidance for a ~22% effective tax rate, against a YTD actual rate of 24.4%, mechanically implies a Q4 tax rate of ~13.5%. This tax catch-up alone contributes approximately $0.40-$0.50 of positive variance that Street models using a standard 23% rate are missing. Furthermore, the consensus estimate implies a ~35% YoY decline in Comparable EPS (vs Q4 '25 $2.63), which is inconsistent with the ongoing mid-single-digit volume growth in the core Beer business (Modelo/Pacifico) which generates the vast majority of profit.

My forecast of $2.52 (Adjusted) anticipates that the strength in Beer and the tax provision tailwind will overwhelmingly offset the drag from Wine & Spirits, where I have already priced in a -11% revenue decline based on recent negative signals from Diageo. The divergence between my $2.52 forecast and the $1.72 consensus is largely structural: I am banking on the realization of tax assets/benefits to hit FY targets, whereas the Street is likely straight-lining operational weakness.

I would revisit this thesis if management had pre-announced a change to FY tax guidance or if Nielsen data for Modelo showed a sudden deceleration in February (which it has not). The only credible threat to this 'beat' is a massive, unexpected 'kitchen sink' cleanup by the new CEO, Nicholas Fink, but such charges typically hit GAAP results rather than the Adjusted EPS figure compared here.

My Q4 FY2026 EPS estimate of ¥38.50 remains 6.9% above Street consensus of ¥36.03, driven primarily by the market's systematic underappreciation of Seven & i's aggressive share count reduction program. The math is straightforward: shares outstanding have declined from 2.60B in Q4 FY25 to 2.44B in Q3 FY26 - a 6.2% reduction in just three quarters. Assuming continued buyback activity at a conservative ¥89B quarterly pace (well below Q3's exceptional ¥162.5B), I project share count declining to 2.38B, providing a mechanical 2.5% tailwind to EPS vs Q3. On the operational side, I expect Q4 seasonal strength to drive revenue to ¥2.475T (+1.9% QoQ) with operating margin expanding to 6.0% from Q3's 4.8% on fixed cost leverage. The key uncertainty is gross margin - Q3's 29.1% was unusually high (vs Q2's 19.3% and Q1's 17.4%), and I'm conservatively assuming normalization to 26.5%. Recent Kroger and Costco results reinforce healthy US retail demand, providing positive read-through for 7-Eleven North America's holiday quarter performance. The Couche-Tard acquisition noise remains in the background but has not materially impacted operations.

What would change my view: If gross margin collapses back to sub-20% levels seen in Q1-Q2, or if buyback activity materially slows, my above-consensus call would be at risk. Conversely, if Q3's elevated gross margin persists and buybacks remain aggressive, there's upside to ¥42+. The Street appears to be using a more conservative share count assumption and may be underweighting the Q4 seasonal operating leverage - these are the primary sources of my differentiated view.

forecasts.thesis:
My ¥39.0 EPS estimate for Seven & i Holdings Q4 FY2026 remains unchanged from my prior forecast, reflecting continued solid execution across the core convenience store franchise despite ongoing M&A uncertainty with Couche-Tard. The investment thesis centers on three key pillars: (1) stable low-single-digit same-store sales growth in both Japan and North America, supported by resilient consumer spending as confirmed by Kroger's Q4 2025 results showing 2% identical sales growth and Costco's strong Q2 2026 performance with continued market share gains; (2) aggressive capital return via the buyback program that has reduced shares outstanding by approximately 10% YTD to an expected 2.35B diluted shares by Q4 end; and (3) gross margin normalization to approximately 25% from Q3's elevated 29% level, which reflects typical quarterly variation rather than structural improvement.

The Wall Street consensus EPS of $0.19 is clearly erroneous—likely a currency conversion or data aggregation error—and should be completely ignored in favor of yen-denominated fundamental analysis. Historical EPS has ranged from ¥19 to ¥42 over the past four quarters, with Q4 typically showing strong seasonal performance (Q4 2025 delivered ¥42 EPS). My ¥39.0 estimate implies a modest YoY decline from Q4 2025's ¥42, reflecting normalization of gross margins and conservative assumptions around the superstore segment recovery, partially offset by share count reduction from buybacks.

Key risks to my thesis include: (1) potential management distraction from the unresolved Couche-Tard acquisition situation, which could impact operational focus; (2) any sudden US consumer weakness, though recent retail earnings suggest this remains a low probability; and (3) currency volatility affecting translation of North American earnings. I would revise my estimate lower if Q4 gross margins fall below 24% or if same-store sales turn negative in either geography. Conversely, stronger-than-expected holiday season performance in Japan or accelerated buyback execution could drive upside to ¥42-43.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.51 remains 7.3% below Street consensus of $0.55, driven by my conviction that analysts are systematically underweighting the mechanical tax rate normalization headwind. Q4 2025's reported EPS of $0.52 benefited from an anomalously low 2.6% effective tax rate ($109M on $4.26B pretax income), which AT&T's 10-K explicitly attributes to discrete tax benefits that will not recur. With management guiding to a 21% effective tax rate for full-year 2026, the tax expense alone should increase by ~$890M sequentially assuming similar pretax income, translating to roughly $0.12 of EPS headwind. The Street consensus appears to be anchoring to the Q4 beat rather than doing the math on normalized taxes.

The new AI-powered app launch announced today is a customer experience enhancement that is neutral to near-term financials - it consolidates existing functionality rather than driving incremental revenue or reducing costs materially in Q1. Meanwhile, the fundamental business remains stable: I expect mobility service revenue to grow 2-3% YoY on continued ARPU expansion and modest net adds, fiber to add ~250K subscribers supporting 15% YoY growth in that segment, while equipment revenue declines ~35% QoQ from the Q4 holiday peak consistent with historical seasonality. Business wireline continues its secular decline at ~4% YoY, partially offset by enterprise 5G/fiber wins.

What would change my view: If management were to signal additional discrete tax benefits carrying into Q1 (they have not), or if the company disclosed a structural change to their tax position, I would need to revise higher. Additionally, if equipment revenue proves more resilient than the typical seasonal decline (perhaps from iPhone cycle dynamics), that would add upside. However, absent new information contradicting the 21% ETR guidance, I maintain high conviction in my below-consensus estimate.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 FY2026 forecast of -$0.03 diluted EPS on $365M revenue represents a dramatically different view than the stale Street consensus of -$0.22 EPS. The consensus figure is fundamentally anchored on historical periods that included massive goodwill impairments ($1.75B in Q4 2025, $1.14B in Q3 2025) that are non-recurring events. Looking at normalized operations, Tilray has achieved near-breakeven for two consecutive quarters (Q1 2026: -$0.003, Q2 2026: -$0.02 excluding working capital adjustments). The business has been transformed - beverage alcohol is now the majority of revenue at 55% vs cannabis at 25%, and the complete global BrewDog consolidation (UK, Ireland, Australia, and now US as of March 16-17) provides a clear path to management's $500M annual beverage target.

The key variant perception is that Wall Street is treating Tilray like a struggling cannabis company when it has effectively become a global beverage platform with cannabis optionality. The Breckenridge Distillery partnership with Cheba Hut (announced 3/18) exemplifies the beverage-first strategy. The BrewDog US acquisition bringing Columbus brewery, three Ohio pubs, hotel, and Las Vegas flagship creates North America's 4th largest craft brewer. I'm projecting $200M in beverage revenue (up 85% YoY) including ~$25M partial quarter from BrewDog US. Integration costs will elevate SG&A to ~$108M, but this is investment in scale, not operational deterioration.

What would change my view: (1) If BrewDog integration costs significantly exceed projections (>$30M one-time), EPS could deteriorate to -$0.07+; (2) If US craft beer market decline accelerates beyond current -3% trends; (3) If ATM dilution accelerates beyond my 565M share assumption. The institutional flows are mixed - Caitong increased stake significantly while Quinn and Luxor reduced positions - suggesting the market hasn't reached consensus on the transformation thesis. My medium conviction reflects execution uncertainty on simultaneous four-region integration, but the fundamental direction is clearly positive.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.01 remains 50% below Wall Street's $0.02 consensus, driven by my fundamental disagreement about Tanzania's mining tax regime that I believe the Street continues to underappreciate. The Q1 2026 reported 111% effective tax rate was NOT an anomaly but reflects the structural reality of mining in Tanzania - including 6% production royalties on gross revenue, withholding taxes on gold exports, and deferred tax timing that creates persistent tax volatility. Management has now been silent on taxes for 27+ days since the February 19 investor roadshow, with no public guidance despite multiple analyst interactions and price target raises. This silence on a critical earnings driver, following a quarter where tax expense exceeded pre-tax income, suggests no positive resolution is imminent.

The operational story remains strong - Q2's record 7,453oz production (+13% QoQ) validates Buckreef's ramp trajectory, and the $21M warrant exercise has transformed the balance sheet with an estimated ~$32M cash position. However, gold price normalization from Q1's exceptional $3,860/oz realized price to ~$2,850/oz creates a 26% ASP headwind that partially offsets volume gains. Combined with 6-7% share dilution from warrant conversions (~20M new shares), I calculate net income of ~$3.8M on an effective tax rate of 55%, yielding EPS of ~$0.01.

I would revise my estimate upward if: (1) management provides concrete guidance showing effective tax rate below 45%, (2) gold prices rally above $3,100/oz sustained, or (3) Q2 production materially exceeds 8,000oz. Conversely, downside risk exists if Tanzania imposes additional mining levies or if the deferred tax liability continues to unwind unfavorably. The Street's $0.02 consensus appears to embed an unrealistic 30-35% effective tax rate that ignores the demonstrated structural tax burden of Tanzanian gold mining operations.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.16 is 3.6% above Street consensus of $1.12, reflecting a differentiated view that UPS's Fit to Serve transformation is delivering sustainable operating leverage that the market continues to underappreciate amid the noise around Amazon volume reductions. While Q4 2025's 10.8% domestic volume decline alarmed investors and contributed to the stock's 11% pullback, the more important signal was the 11.1% operating margin achieved despite this headwind - demonstrating that management's network optimization is working. My analysis suggests Q1 volume declines moderate to approximately -8% as the Amazon reduction reaches a more stable run-rate, while revenue per piece continues improving 3-4% from mix shift toward higher-value shipments.

The key variant perception is that Street models are too focused on top-line volume trends and missing the margin story. Historical data shows Q1 is seasonally the weakest quarter (Q1 2025 operating income was $1.67B vs. $2.73B in Q4), but the transformation benefits should provide a 40-50bps cushion relative to prior-year performance. The Middle East airspace closure creates a real $50-75M fuel headwind, but emergency surcharges are offsetting approximately 60% of this impact. Supply Chain Solutions continues to benefit from healthcare logistics strength and SMB demand, providing diversification away from domestic package weakness.

What would change my view: If Amazon volume reduction accelerates beyond the planned 50% cut, stranded network costs could overwhelm transformation benefits. Similarly, if FedEx's aggressive cost-cutting translates into sustained price competition, it could compress UPS's revenue per piece gains. I'm at medium conviction because while the transformation thesis is supported by Q4 results, Q1 is inherently harder to forecast given seasonal patterns and ongoing macro uncertainty around trade policy and freight demand.

The renewable diesel segment remains a structural drag (~$150M/quarter loss), but this is well-understood by the market. My conviction is HIGH given the clear disconnect between current refining fundamentals and consensus estimates that appear to reflect historical seasonal weakness no longer present in the data.

While institutional accumulation has been notably strong (Danske Bank's $161M new position, Stance Capital up 137%, multiple wealth managers significantly increasing stakes), I believe the Street is pricing in overly optimistic Frontier contribution of $2.1B+ when my analysis suggests $1.85B is more realistic given typical first-quarter integration friction, systems migration complexities, and customer transition challenges. The CEO's Q4 acknowledgment that integration would take time validates this conservative stance.

The key differentiated insight driving my below-consensus view centers on three factors: (1) Frontier's first full quarter will face meaningful integration costs (~$200-250M) that Street models appear to underweight, (2) Q1 seasonal working capital pressures historically depress cash generation and operating leverage, and (3) the January network outage aftermath continues to create customer retention friction that management has not fully quantified. However, I've modestly reduced my estimate from $1.19 to $1.18 after reviewing the strong institutional accumulation patterns, which suggest sophisticated investors see value but also validate that near-term operational challenges remain.

What would change my view: If March wireless subscriber data shows better-than-expected churn normalization (sub-1.0% monthly churn), I would revise upward. Similarly, if Frontier contribution in the quarter exceeds $2.0B with integration costs below $150M, the Street's more optimistic view would be validated. The $21.5B FCF guidance for 2026 provides confidence in underlying operational momentum, but Q1 is typically the weakest quarter for cash generation, which supports my conservative near-term positioning.

forecasts.thesis:
I maintain a bearish variant view ($1.13 EPS vs $1.23 Consensus) predicated on the collision of two structural headwinds: maximum leverage and operational impairment. Wall Street is under-modeling the interest expense drag generated by the Q4 2025 debt explosion (Total Debt up $30B YoY to $200B). While the $19B cash pile offers some interest income offset, the net interest expense will still rise ~15% YoY, shaving roughly $0.06 off EPS compared to consensus models that simply extrapolate operating trends.

Furthermore, the February 2026 network outage is a material event that I have priced in as a $180M revenue headwind (service credits) and a margin compressor. Consensus likely treats this as 'noise', but in a commoditized telecom market, such events trigger measurable churn and credit issuance that flows directly to the bottom line. My 3-statement model specifically accounts for this via reduced Service Revenue and wider 'Other non-operating' expenses.

I would be proven wrong if VZ management utilizes the $19B cash hoard for an immediate, massive debt paydown early in the quarter (negating the interest drag) or if the outage credits were deferred to Q2. However, given the CEO's public apology urgency, Q1 recognition is the prudent assumption.

forecasts.thesis:
My forecast is modestly below the $1.23 consensus at $1.21 EPS on ~$34.0B revenue. The Street’s upside case still appears more narrative-driven (FCF/deleveraging/dividend) than driven by new, quantified Q1 operating KPIs in the provided dataset, so I’m not underwriting a step-change in Q1 margin flow-through.

The key swing is profitability, not revenue. I model modest YoY revenue growth (vs. Q1 2025 revenue of $33.48B) from wireless service price/mix, but assume promotional/retention intensity and customer-care remediation keep operating leverage contained, while net interest expense remains a sizable headwind (modeled interest expense ~$1.62B). Management’s acknowledgement of a recent network outage increases the probability of Q1 credits/care costs, which can be material in a quarter where the Street is leaning to a cleaner margin story.

I would change my view if Verizon discloses or evidence emerges of (1) materially better net adds/churn than implied by the competitive backdrop, (2) clear reduction in promo intensity translating to higher equipment profitability, or (3) outage remediation costs being immaterial. Conversely, larger-than-expected credits/care actions or an aggressive competitive response would push EPS below $1.20 even if revenue holds up.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $2.31 represents a 3.6% premium to Street consensus of $2.23, reflecting continued conviction in Western Digital's AI-driven enterprise HDD supercycle combined with improved near-term sentiment signals. Today's 11.24% stock rally, driven by expanded buyback authorization and Cantor Fitzgerald's +400% position increase, suggests institutional sentiment is shifting more bullish than previously feared. While I maintain the mixed institutional signal narrative (Kingdon/Holocene profit-taking), the Fred Alger +4,924% increase and Cantor's aggressive buying indicate sophisticated money sees value despite elevated prices.

The key differentiated insight driving my above-consensus view is that gross margin compression concerns appear overdone. While I previously modeled 45.0% gross margin based on Morgan Stanley conference commentary about supply chain costs, the favorable mix shift toward higher-margin enterprise HDDs (where WDC has pricing power given strategic importance to AI infrastructure) should offset input cost pressures, supporting 45.3% gross margin. Revenue growth of 6.3% QoQ to $3.21B is supported by CEO Tan's commentary that customers now view HDDs as 'strategic components' rather than commodities - this pricing power dynamic is underappreciated.

My conviction is medium-high but I acknowledge risks: the Seagate sector weakness (-3.25%) and Intel CPU shortage could signal broader tech supply chain constraints that eventually impact WDC. If Q3 guidance disappoints or enterprise HDD orders show sequential decline, I would revisit my premium to consensus. However, the structural AI demand thesis remains intact and WDC's aggressive capital return program (~$600M/quarter buybacks, new dividend) provides EPS support even in a slower growth scenario.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 WFC EPS estimate of $1.59 is 1.9% above the Street consensus of $1.56, driven by a differentiated view on share count reduction and expense normalization that I believe the Street is systematically underweighting. The market appears to be overly focused on NII headwinds from Fed rate cuts while underappreciating two key offsets: (1) Wells Fargo's aggressive $5B/quarter buyback pace is reducing diluted shares from 3.22B in Q4 to an estimated 3.17B in Q1 - this ~1.6% reduction provides meaningful EPS accretion that consensus models often lag in capturing; and (2) Q4's elevated operating expenses ($13.98B) included one-time SG&A items that should normalize to ~$13.50B in Q1, providing $300-400M of cost relief.

The key variant view centers on NII trajectory: while I project NII declining 9.2% QoQ to $11.2B (reflecting continued Fed cut impacts and deposit beta lag), this is slightly better than my prior estimate of $11.15B based on more stable loan demand signals and slower-than-expected deposit repricing. Non-interest income should benefit from Q1 seasonal strength in wealth management and elevated trading activity given market volatility through mid-March. The March 6 termination of the 2018 enforcement action is a positive signal for the longer-term asset cap removal narrative (potentially H2 2026), though not an immediate earnings driver.

What could prove me wrong: If deposit betas accelerate faster than expected (driving NII to $11.0B or below), or if credit provisions need to rise above $1.3B on CRE weakness, my estimate would be too high. The Street may also be correctly pricing in execution risk on the expense normalization that I'm dismissing. I maintain medium conviction given the inherent uncertainty in rate sensitivity models and the opacity of near-term credit dynamics.

I would revisit this thesis if Operating Expenses balloon >$15B without commensurate revenue growth, indicating that the cost of re-starting the growth engine is higher than anticipated. forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.64 represents a $0.06 (3.8%) premium to the $1.58 Wall Street consensus, driven by differentiated insights the Street is systematically underweighting. The primary driver is the sustained Brent crude environment at $79-80/bbl through mid-March versus Q4's $73/bbl average - this alone provides approximately $2.0-2.2B in incremental upstream revenue that consensus has been slow to incorporate following the Q4 miss. The Q4 disappointment (-7.8% surprise) was driven by transitory factors including Gulf Coast weather disruptions and an abnormally low 17.7% effective tax rate that masked underlying operational weakness. With these headwinds normalizing and Guyana's automated drilling breakthrough reducing lifting costs 8-12%, the upstream segment is poised for a strong recovery.

The Street appears anchored to the Q4 miss narrative while missing the structural improvements in Exxon's cost position. The Guyana automation milestone is particularly significant - this represents the world's first fully automated geological well placement, providing sustainable margin improvement not yet priced into consensus estimates. Combined with Payara operating at full 220k bpd capacity and Yellowtail progressing on schedule, the Guyana production complex is delivering better-than-expected economics. Multiple analyst target increases to $163-186 and the stock's 24% YTD rally suggest institutional investors are recognizing this value, but EPS estimates have lagged price action.

What could prove me wrong: (1) OPEC+ policy surprise causing a sharp oil price correction - each $5/bbl decline would reduce my estimate by $0.20-0.25; (2) Refining margins deteriorating beyond my $12-13/bbl crack spread assumption; (3) Tax rate normalization coming in higher than my 29% assumption. The chemical segment remains a known headwind from Asian oversupply, but this is well-understood and priced. My conviction is medium-high given the clear oil price tailwind, but I'm watching OPEC+ developments closely as the key swing factor.

YASKAWA's Motion Control segment, particularly sensitive to Chinese factory automation spending, is unlikely to see the robust recovery the Street appears to be pricing in. Additionally, the robotics segment's auto exposure faces structural headwinds as EV transition disrupts traditional industrial robot demand patterns.

My conviction remains medium given limited company-specific news flow and earnings visibility constraints. I would revise higher if: (1) Management provides explicit margin recovery guidance above 11%, (2) China PMI data shows sustained improvement above 50, or (3) inventory levels decline meaningfully below ¥205B indicating demand recovery. Conversely, I would revise lower if China demand deteriorates further or if currency headwinds emerge from yen strengthening.

(2) Margin pressure is intensifying: gross margin is projected at 33.3% (down from Q3's 34.1%) due to cost inflation, and interest expense remains elevated at ~$475M, squeezing operating income to ~$9.1B. (3) Data reliability risks from the Q2 outlier undermine trend analysis, but excluding it, the business shows steady but softening performance. I differ from consensus by emphasizing the persistent financing cost drag and refined handling of the outlier, while the Street appears to ignore the glaring revenue discrepancy and margin compression.

Key data points driving my view: historical revenue (excluding Q2) trends around $135-144B; interest expense has averaged ~$470M in recent quarters; recent industrial news from competitors like Kadant and Hyster-Yale shows mixed results but no positive catalysts for Yaskawa. My EPS bridge starts with $135B revenue, applies a 33.3% gross margin, subtracts SG&A of ~$35.9B (26.6% of revenue), interest expense of $475M, and a 22.5% tax rate to arrive at net income of ~$6.88B and EPS of $39.5.

What would make me change my mind: If the Q2 2026 outlier is corrected to align with the $135B+ range, indicating stronger underlying growth, or if interest expense drops materially below $400M due to debt repayment. However, given the current data integrity issues and lack of positive catalysts, my bearish adjustment stands.

forecasts.thesis:
My variant view remains that the cached Street EPS ($46.39) bakes in a cleaner return to the prior-year Q4 profitability peak than the recent run-rate supports. In the provided history, Q3 2026 operating income is $9.85B on $134.79B revenue (~7.3% operating margin) versus Q4 2025 operating income of $15.84B on $143.99B (~11.0%). Without company-specific guidance/backlog evidence in the dataset, I model a seasonal Q4 revenue rebound to ~$140.8B but only a partial margin recovery (operating margin ~9.2%), producing EPS of ~$39.

Key datapoints driving this are (1) the step-down in operating margin from Q4 2025 to Q3 2026, suggesting mix/absorption isn’t automatically normalizing, and (2) the persistent inconsistency in the dataset’s scale (notably Q2 2026 and cached consensus revenue), which argues for conservatism and focusing on relative margin/seasonality rather than anchoring to consensus.

I would change my view if we received concrete evidence of a robotics order inflection (backlog acceleration, book-to-bill improving) or explicit margin guidance implying a return toward ~11%+ operating margin; conversely, confirmation of weaker China/EV capex would push me lower on both revenue and margin.

risks: Data quality/units mismatch (historical statements in ~$B scale vs cached consensus revenue in ~$B but far smaller) could distort comparisons and margin inference
FX/non-operating volatility could swing pretax income by ~$0.5B–$1.0B (≈$2–$4 EPS equivalent in this dataset’s scale)
Order timing/China automation cycle uncertainty could shift quarterly revenue by ~1–3% (≈$1.4B–$4.2B)
margin_factors: Gross margin partial recovery vs Q3 but not a full snapback to Q4 2025 peak (mix/absorption caution)
SG&A held near recent run-rate (limited opex leverage in model)
Non-operating/FX treated as swing factor; modeled modest net benefit vs Q3 but not a repeat of best-case
revenue_drivers: Robotics: modest Q4 seasonal rebound vs Q3 but still below prior-year peak demand, limiting YoY growth
Motion Control: steadier baseline with mild sequential uplift; mix not assumed to improve materially
System Engineering/Other: small seasonal uplift; not enough to move consolidated revenue meaningfully

forecasts.thesis: Consensus EPS $46.39 / rev $0.88B is trapped in Q2 data glitch and herding to industrial slowdown narrative, ignoring Yaskawa's robotics dominance in AI-driven manufacturing/reshoring capex cycle; peers like Kadant (record Q4/upbeat '26), Kinaxis (record growth), HY materials handling strength, Schneider automation highs confirm no weakness, with Q3 inventory buildup priming Q4 deliveries. We project +12% QoQ rev seasonality (historical Q4 peak) to $152B, EPS $52.8 on margin expansion to 11%+. Bullish thesis holds absent broad capex pull-forward, which peers refute; would pivot on Yaskawa-specific weakness like China tariffs hitting orders.
